newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu refuses to hold Zaire peace talks at sea.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu refuses to hold Zaire peace talks at sea.

text.p: Doubts grew over a planned meeting between embattled Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel chief Laurent Kabila after a U.S. diplomat said Mobutu had rejected a proposal to hold the talks at sea.

The diplomat, on the entourage of U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson, said Mobutu had told Richardson on Tuesday he would not attend the talks on board a ship offered by South African President Nelson Mandela.

"Mobutu told Richardson there is no way he would be travelling to a ship for talks with Kabila," the diplomat said after talks between Kabila and the envoy. "So once again the venue for the face-to-face meeting remains a problem."
Mobutu, who has cancer, has ruled out South Africa as a venue as too far. Kabila ruled out Congo's capital Brazzaville, over the river from Kinshasa, and Gabon on security grounds.
South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad expressed surprise that Mobutu was not willing to meet with Kabila onboard the South African naval vessel.
"As far as we are concerned there was agreement in principle that the Outeniqua would be a venue acceptable to both sides," Pahad told South African radio.

"The urgency of the situation necessitates that the talks start very quickly...we would urge both parties not to hesitate anymore, and not to cause anymore delays, and move quickly to the negotiating table," he said.
A meeting would be the first between the two arch-rivals. Kabila's forces have captured half the vast central African state since October and are advancing on the capital Kinshasa.
Kabila says talks must be brief and only discuss Mobutu's resignation, otherwise the rebel army will remove him by force.
Richardson, met Mobutu in Kinshasa on Tuesday before flying to rebel-held Lubumbashi for talks with Kabila.
On Wednesday he was heading to the city of Kisangani to assess the plight of Rwandan refugees and would later fly to Kinshasa for a second round of talks with Mobutu.
Kabila told Richardson in Lubumbashi that he was willing to be flexible on a 60-day deadline he has given the United Nations to repatriate all Rwandan refugees provided he saw progress.
"We want to see seriousness on the part of the U.N. that repatriation is actually taking place," Kabila told Reuters.
He said he was still committed to an independent team investigating alleged killings in the refugee camps but wanted rebels to be represented and consulted on its composition.
Richardson might also visit Angola, accused by Kinshasa of invading Zaire to back the ethnic Tutsi-dominated rebels.

Richardson met Kabila late on Tuesday and his aide said the envoy raised concerns about Rwandan Hutu refugees. Kabila promised aid agencies access to the refugees, the aide said. The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda that year.
Kabila told Reuters before his talks with Richardson that pluralist elections could only be held after Mobutu stepped down or was overthrown.

"There will be no compromise over the departure, through the battlefield or at talks, of Mobutu, his system and his henchmen," he said. "Mobutu and everything he represents must go before we can think of holding elections."
Kabila said his rebels were advancing by road on Kinshasa after capturing Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) from the capital. "We have advanced beyond Kikwit. Our destination is Kinshasa."
